# Hypocalcemia

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Fluids, electrolytes, and acid-base disorders > Hypocalcemia*

[Original Article Link](/library/Hg0K92)

---

## Summary

Hypocalcemia is a state of low serum <u>calcium</u> levels (total <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> < 8.5 mg/dL or ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> < 4.65 mg/dL ). <u>Total calcium</u> comprises physiologically-active <u>ionized calcium</u> as well as <u>anion</u>-bound and protein-bound, physiologically-inactive <u>calcium</u>. <u>Calcium</u> plays an important role in various cellular processes in the body, such as stabilizing the <u>resting membrane potential</u> of cells, <u>cell signaling</u>, coagulation, and <u>hormone</u> release. In addition to hormonal control by <u>parathyroid hormone</u> (<u>PTH</u>) and <u>calcitriol</u>, <u>calcium homeostasis</u> is also influenced by <u>serum protein</u> levels and acid-base status, both of which impact the <u>ratio</u> of protein-bound <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> to ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> in the serum. Severity and chronicity of <u>calcium</u> deficiency in addition to the patient's age and comorbidities contribute to the overall clinical presentation of hypocalcemia. Symptoms are variable; the most characteristic features include prolongation of the <u>QT interval</u> and signs of neuromuscular excitation (e.g., <u>tetany</u>, <u>carpopedal spasm</u>, <u>paresthesias</u>). Management consists of <u>calcium</u> supplementation and identifying and treating the underlying cause.

---

## Definitions

* Hypocalcemia: <u>total serum calcium</u> concentration < 8.5 mg/dL or ionized (free) <u>calcium</u> concentration < 4.65 mg/dL [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)

* Severe hypocalcemia: <u>total serum calcium</u> concentration â¤ 7.5 mg/dL, or ionized (free) <u>calcium</u> concentration < 3.6 mg/dL [[2]](/library/cQbaEt)

* Factitious hypocalcemia: an asymptomatic decrease in <u>total calcium</u> with a normal ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> level (typically occurs due to low <u>serum protein</u> levels)

---

## Calcium homeostasis and calcium physiology

### Total and <u>ionized calcium</u> concentrations




* Total calcium: the total amount of <u>calcium</u> circulating in the serum, comprising protein-bound, <u>anion</u>-bound, and <u>ionized calcium</u>

* Approx. 40% of the <u>total serum calcium</u> is bound to <u>proteins</u> (mostly <u>albumin</u>) and is physiologically inactive. [[3]](/library/BFXz4-)

* <u>Hypoproteinemia</u> (due to, e.g., <u>nephrotic syndrome</u>, <u>liver cirrhosis</u>, severe <u>malnutrition</u>, <u>malabsorption</u>) → ↓ total <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> level but ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> level is unaffected;   → <u>factitious hypocalcemia</u>

* <u>pH</u> influences the binding of <u>calcium</u> to <u>serum proteins</u>.

* ↑ <u>pH</u> → ↓ H<sup>+</sup> in serum binding to <u>proteins</u> → ↑ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> binding to <u>proteins</u> → ↓ ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> concentration compensatory ↑ <u>PTH</u>

* ↓ <u>pH</u> → ↑ H<sup>+</sup> in serum binding to <u>proteins</u> → ↓ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> binding to <u>proteins</u> → ↑ ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> concentration compensatory ↓ <u>PTH</u>

* Ionized calcium: the <u>calcium</u> fraction that is not bound to any <u>proteins</u> but is physiologically active

* ∼ 45% of the <u>total serum calcium</u> [[3]](/library/BFXz4-)

* Functions as the main regulator of <u>PTH</u> secretion

* <u>PTH</u> secretion is influenced by <u>pH</u> variations but not by changes in <u>albumin</u> levels.

* An excess causes true <u>hypercalcemia</u> whereas a deficiency causes true hypocalcemia.





> [!NOTE]
> To remember the effect <u>pH</u> has on <u>PTH</u>, think: ↑ <u>pH</u> = ↑ PTH and ↓ <u>pH</u> = ↓ PTH.




### The physiological role of <u>calcium</u> [[4]](/library/Lvaw05)




* Ionized <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> is responsible for stabilizing the <u>resting membrane potential</u> of cells.

* ↓ Serum <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> → ↑ membrane excitability

* ↑ Serum <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> → ↓ membrane excitability

* Acts as a <u>second messenger</u> in signaling pathways

* <u>Cofactor</u> for several enzymes (e.g., <u>phospholipase A</u>, <u>gamma-glutamyltransferase</u>)

* Required for the promotion of <u>coagulation pathways</u>





### Calcium homeostasis




<u>Calcium homeostasis</u> is a complex process, involving many organs (<u>kidneys</u>, <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>, bones, <u>liver</u>, and <u>skin</u>) and <u>hormones</u> (<u>PTH</u>, <u>calcitonin</u>, <u>vitamin D</u>).




| <u>Hormone</u> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Effect on serum [<u>calcium</u>] | Effect on serum [<u>phosphate</u>] | Mechanism of action | Regulation |  |
| <br>Parathyroid hormone<br> | ↑ | ↓ | <br><br>* <u>Kidneys</u><br><br>* Increases <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> reabsorption in the <u>distal</u> tubule<br><br>* Decreases <u>phosphate</u> reabsorption in the <u>proximal convoluted tubules</u><br><br>* Increases active <u>vitamin D</u> (<u>calcitriol</u>) production via stimulation of <u>1-alpha-hydroxylase</u> synthesis in the <u>kidneys</u><br><br>* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u>: indirectly increases <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> absorption via increased <u>1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D</u> (<u>calcitriol</u>) synthesis in the <u>kidneys</u><br><br>* Bone: releases <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> and <u>phosphate</u> from the bones<br><br>* <u>PTH</u> increases the expression of <u>RANKL</u> on <u>osteoblasts</u>.<br><br>* <u>RANKL</u> binds the <u>osteoclastic</u> <u>RANK</u> <u>receptor</u>, which increases <u>osteoclast</u> activity, and results in increased bone resorption and <u>calcium</u> release.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>PTH</u> secretion is stimulated by:<br><br>* Decrease in serum <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u><br><br>* <u>Hyperphosphatemia</u><br><br>* Mild <u>hypomagnesemia</u> (e.g., due to <u>chronic diarrhea</u>, <u>IBD</u>, <u>loop diuretics</u>, <u>alcohol</u>)<br><br>* Low <u>calcitriol</u> levels<br><br>* <u>PTH</u> secretion is inhibited by:<br><br>* Increase in serum <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u><br><br>* Marked <u>hypomagnesemia</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Calcitriol</u> (<u>vitamin D<sub>3</sub></u>)<br> | ↑ | ↑ | <br><br>* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u>: increases Сa<sup>2+</sup> and <u>phosphate</u> absorption<br><br>* <u>Kidneys</u>: increases <u>phosphate</u> and Сa<sup>2+</sup> reabsorption<br><br>* Bone: enhances bone mineralization<br><br>* For more information, see <u>vitamin D synthesis</u> and <u>vitamin D deficiency</u>.<br><br><br> | <br>* A decrease in serum <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> indirectly ↑ <u>calcitriol</u> via ↑ <u>PTH</u>.<br><br> |
| <br>Calcitonin<br> | ↓ | ↓ | <br><br>* Opposes the effects of <u>PTH</u><br><br>* Inhibits bone resorption, decreasing serum <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u><br><br><br> | <br>* An increase in serum <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> results in ↑ <u>calcitonin</u> secretion.<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> The acronym “<u>PTH</u>” describes the action of <u>parathyroid hormone</u>: P = <u>Phosphate</u> T = Trashing H = <u>Hormone</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> To remember that <u>calcitonin</u> keeps the <u>calcium</u> in the bones, think: Calci-bone-in!

## Etiology

| Types of hypocalcemia | Etiology | Pathophysiology |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low <u>PTH</u> | <u>Hypoparathyroidism</u> | <br><br>* Surgical removal of the <u>parathyroid glands</u> (<u>thyroidectomy</u>, <u>parathyroidectomy</u>)<br><br>* Autoimmune destruction of the <u>parathyroid glands</u> (e.g., in <u>autoimmune polyglandular syndrome</u>)<br><br>* Congenital disorders of the <u>parathyroid gland</u> (e.g., <u>DiGeorge syndrome</u>)<br><br><br> |
| High <u>PTH</u> (<u>secondary hyperparathyroidism</u>) | <u>Vitamin D deficiency</u> | <br><br>* <u>Malnutrition</u> and <u>malabsorption</u> (e.g., <u>alcoholism</u>, chronic <u>IBD</u>, <u>cystic fibrosis</u>, gastric-bypass)<br><br>* Lack of sunlight exposure<br><br>* Decreased enzymatic <u>hydroxylation</u> to active form (e.g., <u>cirrhosis</u>/<u>liver</u> disease, <u>chronic kidney disease</u>)<br><br>* <u>Vitamin D-dependent rickets</u> (type 1 and type 2)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Chronic kidney disease</u> | <br><br>* ↓ Renal excretion of <u>phosphate</u> → <u>hyperphosphatemia</u> → <u>calcium</u>-<u>phosphate</u> precipitation in tissues → ↓ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u><br><br>* ↓ Renal <u>hydroxylation</u> of <u>vitamin D</u> → ↓ <u>1,25-(OH)<sub>2</sub> vitamin D<sub>3</sub></u> → ↓ intestinal <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> absorption → ↓ <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u><br><br><br> |  |
| Pseudohypoparathyroidism | <br>* <u>PTH</u> resistance<br><br> |  |
| <u>Hyperphosphatemia</u> | <br><br>* ↓ Renal excretion of <u>phosphate</u> (e.g., impaired renal function)<br><br>* Increased <u>phosphate</u> intake (e.g., oral supplements, enemas)<br><br>* Increased tissue breakdown (e.g., <u>tumor lysis syndrome</u>, <u>rhabdomyolysis</u>, <u>crush injury</u>)<br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Acute <u>necrotizing pancreatitis</u> (see <u>acute pancreatitis</u>) | <br>* <u>Calcium</u> soap precipitation in the abdomen<br><br> |  |
| Other | Medications | <br><br>* <u>Loop diuretics</u> increase renal <u>calcium</u> excretion.<br><br>* <u>Calcitonin</u><br><br>* <u>Bisphosphonates</u><br><br>* <u>Glucocorticoids</u><br><br>* <u>Denosumab</u><br><br>* <u>Foscarnet</u><br><br>* <u>Phosphate</u><br><br>* <u>L-asparaginase</u><br><br>* <u>Doxorubicin</u><br><br>* <u>Cisplatin</u><br><br>* <u>Ketoconazole</u><br><br>* <u>Pentamidine</u><br><br>* <u>Cytosine arabinoside</u><br><br>* Gallium <u>nitrate</u><br><br>* Plicamycin<br><br><br> |
| Multiple <u>blood transfusions</u> and <u>hemolysis</u> | <br>* <u>Citrate</u> in <u>blood products</u> chelates serum <u>calcium</u>.<br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Hypomagnesemia</u> (see <u>magnesium</u>) <br> | <br>* <u>Hypomagnesemia</u> → ↓ <u>PTH</u> secretion or induces <u>PTH</u> resistance → hypocalcemia<br><br> |  |
| <u>Hyperventilation</u> | <br>* Redistribution of <u>calcium</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Osteoblastic metastases</u> | <br>* <u>Metastases</u> of primary malignancies (e.g., <u>prostate cancer</u>, <u>small cell lung cancer</u>) in the bone with rapid new bone formation<br><br> |  |
| <u>Renal tubular disorders</u> | <br>* See <u>RTA</u> type 1.<br><br> |  |
| <u>Pseudohypocalcemia</u> | <br>* Due to <u>gadolinium</u> contrast agent or <u>hypoalbuminemia</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Neonatal hypocalcemia</u> | <br>* Due to cessation of <u>placental</u> <u>Ca<sup>2+</sup></u> transfer at <u>birth</u><br><br> |  |
| <u>Hungry bone syndrome</u> | <br>* Hypocalcemia following <u>parathyroidectomy</u> or <u>thyroidectomy</u> despite normal or increased <u>PTH</u><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> Hypocalcemia is most often due to <u>hypoparathyroidism</u> or <u>vitamin D</u> deficiency (e.g., <u>malabsorption</u>, <u>chronic kidney disease</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> Suspect hypocalcemia in the postoperative <u>thyroidectomy</u> patient with new-onset <u>paresthesias</u> and muscle spasms or cramping.

## Clinical features

Manifestations of hypocalcemia are influenced by the severity and chronicity of the hypocalcemia as well as by the patient's age and comorbidities.




### Neurological manifestations [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)[[13]](/library/EpY8rJ)[[14]](/library/IQbYxt)[[15]](/library/7Qb4xt)




* Tetany: increased neuromuscular excitability (when caused by <u>respiratory alkalosis</u> = <u>hyperventilation-induced tetany</u>)

* <u>Paresthesias</u>: typically tingling or pins-and-needles sensation in extremities and/or in the perioral area

* Spasms (e.g., carpopedal spasm  , <u>bronchospasm</u> or <u>laryngospasm</u> ), and cramps (possible in any muscle)

* Stiffness, <u>myalgia</u>

* Maneuvers to elicit latent <u>tetany</u> on <u>physical exam</u>

* Chvostek sign: short contractions (twitching) of the facial muscles elicited by tapping the <u>facial nerve</u> below and in front of <u>the ear</u> (∼ 2 cm <u>ventral</u> to <u>the ear</u> lobe)  [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)

* Trousseau sign: <u>ipsilateral</u> <u>carpopedal spasm</u> occurring several minutes after inflation of a blood pressure cuff to pressures above the systolic blood pressure  [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)

* <u>Seizure</u>: may be the initial or only symptom  [[14]](/library/IQbYxt)





> [!TIP]
> Signs of neuromuscular irritability (e.g., <u>paresthesias</u>, spasms and cramps) are the most characteristic features of hypocalcemia.




![Chvostek's Sign and Trousseau's Sign due to Postoperative Acquired Hypoparathyroidism | NEJM](media/small_63e665108b5372.34697235.jpg)

Chvostek's Sign and Trousseau's Sign due to Postoperative Acquired Hypoparathyroidism | NEJM




### Cardiovascular manifestations [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)[[13]](/library/EpY8rJ)[[14]](/library/IQbYxt)[[15]](/library/7Qb4xt)




* <u>Congestive heart failure</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* <u>Cardiac arrhythmias</u> (symptoms may include <u>palpitations</u>, irregular <u>pulse</u>, <u>syncope</u>)





### Manifestations of chronic hypocalcemia [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)[[13]](/library/EpY8rJ)[[14]](/library/IQbYxt)[[15]](/library/7Qb4xt)




* Psychiatric manifestations (variable and usually mild; may be reversible), such as emotional instability, <u>anxiety</u>, <u>depression</u>, confusion/<u>delirium</u>, hallucinosis, or <u>psychosis</u>

* Ophthalmologic manifestations: <u>papilledema</u> (in severe cases), <u>cataracts</u>, calcifications of the <u>cornea</u>

* Neurological manifestations: <u>pseudotumor cerebri</u>, paradoxical <u>CNS</u> calcifications

* Dental changes: altered morphology, <u>dental enamel</u> <u>hypoplasia</u>

* <u>Growth plate</u> abnormalities and <u>osteomalacia</u>





![Hypocalcemia fact sheet](media/xwek5nrgivze6dp8nommmpyl.jpg)

Hypocalcemia fact sheet

## Diagnosis

### Approach




* Confirm hypocalcemia: Order total and <u>ionized calcium</u> or correct serum <u>calcium</u> for <u>albumin</u> level

* Determine etiology: Obtain serum intact <u>PTH</u> level.

* Elevated <u>PTH</u> levels: Consider and investigate other causes (e.g., <u>renal failure</u>, <u>vitamin D deficiency</u>, medication side effects, familial or genetic disorders).

* Normal or low <u>PTH</u> levels: <u>hypoparathyroidism</u> is the likely cause.





![Diagnosis of hypocalcemia](media/nbco1cjdu757wrelf5113nah.jpg)

Diagnosis of hypocalcemia




> [!WARNING]
> Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is a <u>medical emergency</u> that is potentially fatal, diagnostics should not delay treatment.




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/cQbaEt)[[13]](/library/EpY8rJ)




#### Routine studies




* Confirm true hypocalcemia

* Measure total and <u>ionized calcium</u>

* AND/OR check serum <u>albumin</u> and calculate <u>corrected calcium</u>

* Evaluate for other <u>electrolyte</u> abnormalities

* <u>BMP</u>

* Serum <u>phosphate</u> and <u>magnesium</u>

* <u>ABG</u>/<u>VBG</u>





![Calcium correction for hypoalbuminemia](media/pqd5s6w9f42eo43ct2ytqblm.jpg)

Calcium correction for hypoalbuminemia




#### Additional studies




* Serum intact <u>PTH</u>:

* Indication: best initial study for confirmed hypocalcemia with no clear etiology

* Interpretation

* Low (or normal) <u>PTH</u> suggests <u>hypoparathyroidism</u>

* High <u>PTH</u> suggests <u>parathyroid gland</u> function is preserved

* Further serum studies: conducted based on clinical suspicion

* <u>Alkaline phosphatase</u>

* <u>Amylase</u>

* <u>25-hydroxyvitamin D</u> (<u>calcidiol</u>)

* Urine studies: 24-hour urinary excretion of <u>calcium</u> and <u>magnesium</u>





| <br>Interpretation of laboratory findings in hypocalcemia [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <u>PTH</u> level | Additional findings | Conditions |
| Low <u>PTH</u> | <br>* ↑ <u>Phosphate</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hypoparathyroidism</u> (e.g., postsurgical)<br><br> |
| High <u>PTH</u> | <br><br>* Low or normal <u>phosphate</u><br><br>* ↓ <u>25-hydroxyvitamin D</u> (<u>calcidiol</u>)  [[16]](/library/yoYdeJ)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Vitamin D deficiency</u><br><br> |
| <br>* ↑ <u>Phosphate</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hyperphosphatemia</u><br><br>* Pseudohypoparathyroidism<br><br><br> |  |
| <br><br>* ↑ <u>Phosphate</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Creatinine</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Chronic kidney disease</u><br><br> |  |
| <br>* ↓ <u>Magnesium</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Malabsorption</u> or <u>alcoholism</u><br><br> |  |





> [!TIP]
> The typical laboratory findings of <u>vitamin D deficiency</u> are ↓ <u>calcium</u>, ↓ (or normal) <u>phosphate</u>, and ↑ <u>PTH</u>.




### <u>ECG</u>




* Indication: acute, severe, and/or symptomatic hypocalcemia

* ECG findings of hypocalcemia include: [[14]](/library/IQbYxt)

* Prolonged <u>QT interval</u>

* <u>Ventricular arrhythmias</u>: <u>torsades de pointes</u>, <u>ventricular tachycardia</u>, <u>ventricular fibrillation</u>

* <u>QRS complex</u> and <u>ST-segment</u> changes (may mimic <u>myocardial infarction</u>)

* <u>AV block</u>





![ECG in hypocalcemia](media/ab20f3q7g7ajbcs8vanrgbau.jpg)

ECG in hypocalcemia




### <u>Fundoscopy</u>




* Recommended in severe/symptomatic cases

* Possible findings: <u>papilledema</u>  [[15]](/library/7Qb4xt)

---

## Treatment

The mainstay of therapy of hypocalcemia consists of <u>calcium</u> supplementation and the treatment of the underlying cause.




### <u>Calcium</u> supplementation [[2]](/library/cQbaEt)




<u>Calcium</u> supplementation should be provided based on severity. See “<u>Repletion regimens for hypocalcemia</u>” for more details on <u>calcium</u> supplementation with specific dosages.




* Severe and/or symptomatic hypocalcemia: e.g., <u>tetany</u>, <u>seizures</u>, prolonged <u>QT interval</u>, serum <u>calcium</u> â¤ 7.5 mg/dL 

* IV <u>calcium</u> supplementation: <u>calcium gluconate</u> or <u>calcium</u> <u>chloride</u>

* Continuous <u>telemetry</u>  [[2]](/library/cQbaEt)

* Consider transfer to critical care unit

* Mild and/or chronic hypocalcemia: no symptoms or only mild neuromuscular irritability (e.g., <u>paresthesias</u>), serum <u>calcium</u> 7.6–8.4 mg/dL
* Oral <u>calcium</u> supplementation: <u>calcium</u> <u>citrate</u>, <u>calcium carbonate</u>





> [!WARNING]
> IV <u>calcium</u> can trigger life threatening <u>arrhythmias</u> in patients simultaneously receiving <u>cardiac glycosides</u> (<u>digoxin</u> or digitoxin). [[1]](/library/9lbN_F)




### Treatment of the underlying condition




* <u>Hypoparathyroidism</u>

* <u>Calcium</u> supplementation (See “<u>Repletion regimens for hypocalcemia</u>” and “Treatment” in “<u>Hypoparathyroidism</u>”)

* PLUS <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation

* Secondary to <u>loop diuretics</u>: consider discontinue <u>loop diuretic</u> and change medication to <u>thiazides</u>

* <u>Vitamin D deficiency</u>: <u>vitamin D</u> supplementation

* <u>Hypomagnesemia</u>-induced hypocalcemia: <u>magnesium</u> supplementation (See “<u>Repletion regimens for hypomagnesemia</u>”)

* <u>Hyperphosphatemia</u> in <u>chronic kidney disease</u>: <u>calcium</u> supplementation





> [!NOTE]
> Loop <u>diuretics</u> Lose <u>calcium</u>. Discontinue them in <u>hyp</u>ocalcemia.
